paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn the gods meet in council with Zeus, their king. Athena, who pities Odysseus because he is stuck far away in the home of the nymph Calypso, starts telling them about his many sufferings.

barriers.quote: Dawn rose from her couch beside Tithonus
barriers.my_reading: Dawn is a goddess getting out of bed ('couch' = bed); Tithonus seems to be her husband or lover, but the text never says who he is.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only for who Tithonus is

barriers.quote: herald of light to mortals and immortals alike
barriers.my_reading: Describes Dawn, who announces daylight to humans and gods; because it comes straight after 'Tithonus' it first reads as describing him.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena tells her father Zeus and the other gods, bitterly, that kings might as well be cruel from now on, because Odysseus ruled his people like a kind father and yet every one of them has forgotten him. He is stuck in misery on Calypso's island, she won't let him go, and he has no ship or crew to get home. Now wicked people are plotting to murder his only son Telemachus on his way home from Pylos and Lacedaemon, where he went to look for news of his father.

barriers.quote: I hope there may never be such a thing as a kind and well-disposed ruler any more
barriers.my_reading: A bitter, ironic wish: since being a good king earned Odysseus nothing, rulers may as well be cruel. Taken literally, Athena seems to want tyrants.
barriers.note: the irony has to be inferred from the 'for' clause that follows

barriers.quote: there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Odysseus
barriers.my_reading: Every one of his subjects has forgotten him.
barriers.note: archaic 'not one... but has' construction; on a quick read it can flip to 'not one has forgotten him'

barriers.quote: lying in great pain
barriers.my_reading: Emotional misery (grief, homesickness), not a physical injury; later paragraphs show him weeping on the shore.

barriers.quote: wicked people are trying to murder
barriers.my_reading: Presumably the 'suitors' Zeus names in the next paragraph; who they are is not explained in this Book.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Zeus replies to his daughter: why complain, when she herself sent Telemachus on this trip as part of her plan for Odysseus to get home and take revenge on the suitors? She is perfectly able to protect Telemachus and bring him home safely, so the suitors lying in wait for him will have to hurry back without having killed him.

barriers.quote: Did you not send him there yourself
barriers.my_reading: 'him' is Telemachus and 'there' is Pylos and Lacedaemon, not Odysseus on Calypso's island.
barriers.note: Athena's speech was mostly about Odysseus, so 'him' first reads as Odysseus

barriers.quote: the suitors
barriers.my_reading: The 'wicked people' plotting against Telemachus; the text never says who they are or whom they are courting.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only (men wooing Odysseus's wife); not explained in Books 5-6, presumably set up earlier

barriers.quote: because you thought it would help Odysseus to get home and punish the suitors
barriers.my_reading: Telemachus's trip is part of Athena's larger plan for Odysseus's return and revenge, but how the trip itself helps is not explained.

barriers.quote: the suitors have to come hurrying and scurrying back without having killed him
barriers.my_reading: The suitors have gone out to ambush Telemachus somewhere on his route and will have to return empty-handed; where they are is not said.
barriers.note: phrased as a statement but works as an instruction/intended outcome

paragraphs.paraphrase: Zeus sends his son Hermes, the gods' messenger, to tell Calypso that the gods have decided Odysseus is to go home. He will travel alone, with no god or human escort, and after twenty dangerous days on a raft reach Scheria, land of the Phaeacians, who are close relatives of the gods. They will honour him like a god, send him home by ship, and give him more bronze, gold and clothing than he would have brought home from Troy if he had kept all his share of the loot.

barriers.quote: near of kin to the gods
barriers.my_reading: closely related to the gods

barriers.quote: if he had had all his prize money
barriers.my_reading: His share of the plunder from the sack of Troy, which he evidently lost on the way home.
barriers.note: 'prize money' today suggests contest or lottery winnings

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hermes obeys: he ties on his golden sandals, which let him fly like the wind over land and sea, and takes his wand that can put people to sleep or wake them. He flies over Pieria, then drops to sea level and skims the waves like a cormorant (a sea bird) hunting fish and soaking its feathers in the spray. After a long flight he reaches Calypso's island and walks on to her cave.

barriers.quote: slayer of Argus
barriers.my_reading: A title of Hermes referring to some past deed; the text never says who Argus was.

barriers.quote: like a cormorant that flies fishing every hole and corner of the ocean
barriers.my_reading: Hermes skims the waves like a diving sea bird that searches every part of the sea for fish.
barriers.note: 'cormorant' may be unfamiliar; 'fishing every hole and corner' is an odd phrase

barriers.quote: many a weary wave
barriers.my_reading: The long, wearying stretch of sea he crosses; the waves themselves are not tired.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso is at home, weaving at her loom and singing, with a fragrant fire of cedar and sandalwood on the hearth. Around the cave grow alder, poplar and cypress trees full of nesting owls, hawks and sea birds; a grapevine grows around the entrance, and four streams in channels water beds of violets and greenery. The place is so lovely that even Hermes, a god, stops to admire it before going in.

barriers.quote: shooting her golden shuttle through the warp
barriers.my_reading: Weaving terms: the shuttle carries the thread back and forth through the lengthwise threads (the warp) on the loom. She is weaving.

barriers.quote: sea-crows that do their business in the waters
barriers.my_reading: Sea birds that make their living (catch fish) on the sea. In modern English 'do their business' means going to the toilet, so the line reads as unintended toilet humour.
barriers.note: modern idiom clash; sounds odd aloud; 'sea-crows' is also an unknown bird

barriers.quote: A vine loaded with grapes was trained
barriers.my_reading: The grapevine had been guided to grow along and around the cave entrance (gardening sense of 'trained').

barriers.quote: channels cut fairly close together, and turned this way and that
barriers.my_reading: Four streams start near each other and then run off in different directions through the flower beds.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso recognises Hermes at once, since all gods know each other; Odysseus is not in the cave but, as usual, on the beach weeping and staring at the empty sea. Calypso seats Hermes and asks why he has come, as he rarely visits; she promises to do what he wants if she can, but first offers him food.

barriers.quote: but come inside, and let me set refreshment before you
barriers.my_reading: Probably 'come further in and eat', but Hermes has already gone inside (end of previous paragraph) and been given a seat, so it is unclear where he is.

paragraphs.paraphrase: While speaking, Calypso pulls up a table of ambrosia beside Hermes and mixes him red nectar; he eats and drinks his fill and then answers her.

barriers.quote: a table loaded with ambrosia beside him and mixed him some red nectar
barriers.my_reading: Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods (made clear only in paragraph 15, where they contrast with 'the food that mortals eat'). Why nectar is 'mixed' is not explained.
barriers.note: modern senses (a dessert; flower juice) do not fit

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hermes says that, speaking as one god to another, he will be honest: Zeus sent him, and he would never have come by choice across so much empty sea with no cities of people making offerings, but no god can defy Zeus. Zeus says Calypso is keeping the unluckiest of the men who besieged King Priam's city for nine years and sacked it in the tenth; on the way home they offended Athena, who sent storms that killed all his companions, and he alone drifted here. Zeus orders her to release him at once, because he is fated not to die here but to reach home and his friends again.

barriers.quote: We are speaking god and goddess to one another
barriers.my_reading: Because they are both gods, he will answer her question frankly; the connection is only implied.

barriers.quote: sacrifices or choice victims
barriers.my_reading: 'Victims' are the selected animals killed as offerings to the gods; the modern sense suggests people who have been harmed, or even human sacrifice.

barriers.quote: the city of King Priam
barriers.my_reading: Troy; the text mentions Troy elsewhere but does not connect it to Priam.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only that Priam was king of Troy

barriers.quote: they sinned against Athena, who raised both wind and waves against them
barriers.my_reading: The Greeks offended Athena somehow and she sent a storm. What they did is never said, and it is surprising because Athena is the one pleading for Odysseus in paragraphs 0-1.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only for what the offence was

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso, trembling with rage, says the gods are jealous and cannot bear a goddess openly taking a mortal man as her husband: when Dawn loved Orion, they raged until Artemis killed him, and when Demeter slept with Iasion in a field, Zeus killed Iasion with thunderbolts. She rescued Odysseus when he drifted in alone, clinging to wreckage after Zeus sank his ship with lightning and drowned his crew, and she loved him and wanted to make him immortal. She cannot defy Zeus, so she will let him go, but she has no ship or crew to give him; she will, however, honestly advise him how to get home safely.

barriers.quote: yielded to him in a thrice-plowed fallow field
barriers.my_reading: Demeter had sex with Iasion in a field that had been ploughed three times and left unplanted; the point of the detail is not explained.

barriers.quote: sitting all alone astride a keel
barriers.my_reading: Straddling the bottom beam (keel) of his wrecked ship, i.e. clinging to a piece of wreckage.

barriers.quote: for Zeus had struck his ship with lightning
barriers.my_reading: Calypso says Zeus wrecked him, while Hermes has just said Athena raised the storm; the reader has to reconcile two different accounts.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hermes tells her to send Odysseus away, then, or Zeus will be angry and punish her.

Hermes leaves and Calypso, now under Zeus's orders, goes to find Odysseus on the beach, weeping and dying of homesickness. He has tired of Calypso and sleeps with her at night only because she insists; he spends his days on the rocks and shore, crying and staring out to sea. She comes up close and speaks to him.

barriers.quote: it was she, not he, who would have it so
barriers.my_reading: She wanted it that way; he did not (he sleeps with her unwillingly).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso tells Odysseus he need not waste away in grief any longer, because she is letting him go 'of her own free will' (she does not mention Zeus's order). He should cut timber and build a large raft with a deck; she will stock it with bread, wine and water, give him clothes, and send a favourable wind, if the gods of heaven allow it, since they have more power over such things than she does.

barriers.quote: a large raft with an upper deck
barriers.my_reading: A raft with a raised platform on top; hard to picture how a raft has an 'upper' deck.

barriers.quote: if the gods in heaven so will it—for they know more about these things, and can settle them better than I can
barriers.my_reading: Calypso is a goddess herself but defers to the more powerful gods 'in heaven' (Zeus and his council); how the ranks of gods work is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus shudders and suspects a trick: she cannot really mean to help him if she tells him to cross the sea on a raft, a voyage not even a well-equipped ship with a good wind would attempt. He refuses to board unless she first swears a solemn oath that she is not plotting harm against him.

barriers.quote: well-found ship
barriers.my_reading: a well-equipped, properly fitted-out ship

barriers.quote: you mean me no mischief
barriers.my_reading: you intend me no harm
barriers.note: modern 'mischief' sounds like harmless naughtiness, which undercuts his fear

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso smiles, strokes him, and says that for all his cleverness he is wrong this time. She swears by heaven, earth and the river Styx (the most solemn oath a god can take) that she means him no harm and is advising exactly what she would do in his place, honestly, because she has a heart and pities him.

barriers.quote: the waters of the river Styx
barriers.my_reading: A river the gods swear by; the text says it is their most binding oath but not what or where the Styx is.
barriers.note: outside knowledge: a river of the underworld

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso walks quickly back to her cave with Odysseus following, and he sits in the chair Hermes has just left. She serves him ordinary human food and drink while her maids bring her ambrosia and nectar, and when they have eaten their fill, Calypso speaks.

barriers.quote: her maids
barriers.my_reading: Calypso has servants (presumably other nymphs); they have not been mentioned before, and she has just said she has no 'men' to help.

barriers.quote: they laid their hands on the good things that were before them
barriers.my_reading: They started eating.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Calypso asks Odysseus, son of Laertes, whether he really wants to leave at once, and wishes him luck. If he knew how much suffering lay ahead before he got home, she says, he would stay, live with her and let her make him immortal, however much he longs for the wife he thinks about every day. She is sure she is no less tall or beautiful than his wife, since no mortal woman can compete with a goddess.

barriers.quote: It makes no difference how anxious you may be to see this wife of yours
barriers.my_reading: However much he longs for his wife, if he knew his future he would still choose to stay; the link to the previous sentence is loose.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus asks her not to be angry: he knows his wife Penelope, being mortal, is nowhere near as tall or beautiful as Calypso. Still, he wants to go home above everything, and if a god wrecks him at sea he will endure it, since he has already suffered endlessly on land and sea and this will be one more trouble.

barriers.quote: let this go with the rest
barriers.my_reading: Add this to all the other hardships; not 'let it go / forget it'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The sun sets, and Calypso and Odysseus go into the inner part of the cave and to bed together.

barriers.quote: Presently
barriers.my_reading: Soon afterwards (not 'currently').
barriers.note: archaic sense; recurs in paragraphs 31 and 34

paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn Calypso, in a fine gauzy dress, gold belt and veil, gives Odysseus a big double-edged bronze axe with an olive-wood handle and an adze, and shows him the tallest, driest trees at the far end of the island. He fells twenty trees, trims and squares them, drills them with augers she brings and fastens them with bolts, building a raft as wide as a large ship with a deck, a raised edge, a mast and crossbar, a steering oar, wicker screens against the waves and a load of extra wood. She brings linen, he makes and rigs the sails with ropes, and finally levers the raft down into the sea.

barriers.quote: the rosy-fingered child of morning
barriers.my_reading: A poetic title for Dawn (pink streaks of light like fingers); calling Dawn the 'child of morning' feels circular.

barriers.quote: a sharp adze
barriers.my_reading: a woodworking tool for shaping timber
barriers.note: unfamiliar tool name; only the gist (a tool) is recoverable

barriers.quote: very dry and well seasoned, so as to sail light for him in the water
barriers.my_reading: The wood had dried out, so it would be light and float well.

barriers.quote: squaring them by rule
barriers.my_reading: Cutting the logs into square-edged beams using a straightedge or marked line.

barriers.quote: augers
barriers.my_reading: drills; the text explains that he bored holes with them

barriers.quote: as broad as a skilled shipwright makes the beam of a large vessel
barriers.my_reading: 'Beam' is the width of a ship: the raft is as wide as a big cargo ship. Earlier 'beams of wood' (paragraph 12) meant timbers, so it is easy to read 'beam' as a plank.

barriers.quote: fixed a deck on top of the ribs
barriers.my_reading: the cross-timbers forming the raft's frame

barriers.quote: ran a gunwale all round it
barriers.my_reading: a raised rail or edge along the sides
barriers.note: nautical; pronounced 'gunnel', so aloud it may not match the spelling

barriers.quote: a mast with a yardarm
barriers.my_reading: the crossbar on the mast from which the sail hangs

barriers.quote: wicker hurdles
barriers.my_reading: woven panels of branches set up as a fence or screen along the sides

barriers.quote: then he threw on a quantity of wood
barriers.my_reading: Unclear: perhaps extra brushwood as ballast or padding, or to strengthen the wicker screen.

barriers.quote: making them fast with braces and sheets
barriers.my_reading: Tying the sails in place with the ropes that control them; 'sheets' and 'braces' are ropes, not cloth or straps.
barriers.note: nautical; right after 'linen', 'sheets' reads as cloth

paragraphs.paraphrase: The work takes four days; on the fifth Calypso bathes and dresses him, gives him a skin of dark wine, a bigger skin of water, a bag of food and plenty of meat, and sends a warm favourable wind. He sails, steering with the rudder, and stays awake navigating by the stars (the Pleiades, Bootes and the Bear, also called the Wain, which circles in place opposite Orion and never sinks into the ocean), keeping the Bear on his left as Calypso told him. After seventeen days, on the eighteenth, he sees the faint mountains of the Phaeacian coast, shaped like a shield on the horizon.

barriers.quote: a goatskin full of black wine
barriers.my_reading: A leather bag made from a goat's hide used as a container; 'black' wine means very dark red wine.

barriers.quote: keep the Bear on his left
barriers.my_reading: The Bear is a group of stars (the Great Bear); keeping it on his left sets his course. Only the next sentence makes clear it is in the sky.
barriers.note: which direction this means is outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: the Pleiads, on late-setting Bootes
barriers.my_reading: Names of stars/constellations he steers by; 'late-setting' = it sets late in the night.

barriers.quote: Men also call it the Wain
barriers.my_reading: 'Wain' is an old word for wagon; another name for the Bear constellation.

barriers.quote: alone never dips into the stream of Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: It is the only constellation that never sets below the horizon; 'Oceanus' seems to be the ocean imagined as a river around the world.

barriers.quote: facing Orion
barriers.my_reading: Orion here is the constellation, not the man in Calypso's story (paragraph 9); the text does not link them.

barriers.quote: rising like a shield on the horizon
barriers.my_reading: The distant land looks like a round shield lying on the sea: a low, domed outline.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Poseidon, returning from a visit to the Ethiopians, spots Odysseus sailing from far off, from the mountains of the Solymi, and is furious. He mutters that the other gods changed their minds about Odysseus while he was away, and that Odysseus is now close to the Phaeacians' land, where he is fated to escape his troubles, but he vows Odysseus will still suffer plenty first.

barriers.quote: it made him very angry
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon has a grudge against Odysseus, but neither this Book nor Book 6 says why; he is not even identified as the sea god until paragraph 33.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only for the cause

barriers.quote: returning from the Ethiopians
barriers.my_reading: He had been away visiting a distant people, which is why the other gods could decide without him; why he was there is not said.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Poseidon gathers the clouds, stirs the sea with his trident and unleashes every wind, so that everything goes dark and huge waves rise from all four directions at once. Odysseus despairs: Calypso's warning is coming true, Zeus is blackening the sky, and he is sure to die. He envies the Greeks who died at Troy fighting for the sons of Atreus and wishes he had been killed the day the Trojans pressed him hard in the fight over Achilles' body, since then he would have had a proper funeral and lasting fame instead of this miserable death at sea.

barriers.quote: fell on him
barriers.my_reading: 'him' is Odysseus, although the previous sentence was all about Poseidon; the end of the sentence clears it up.

barriers.quote: How black Zeus is making heaven with his clouds
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus blames Zeus; the reader knows Poseidon caused the storm, but Odysseus does not.
barriers.note: adds to confusion over which god is doing what

barriers.quote: those Danaans who fell before Troy in the cause of the sons of Atreus
barriers.my_reading: 'Danaans' seems to mean the Greek soldiers at Troy, and 'the sons of Atreus' the leaders they fought for; 'fell before Troy' = died in battle outside Troy. None of this is explained.

barriers.quote: pressing me so hard about the dead body of Achilles
barriers.my_reading: In battle the Trojans attacked him fiercely around Achilles' corpse, as the two sides fought over it; 'about' = around, not 'concerning'.

barriers.quote: the Achaeans would have honored my name
barriers.my_reading: The Achaeans appear to be the Greeks again: a second name for the same army in the same speech, not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: A huge wave hits; the raft lurches, Odysseus is flung far overboard and loses the steering oar, and the storm snaps the mast halfway up so that the sail and its crossbar fall into the sea. Dragged down by Calypso's clothes, he stays under a long time, but finally surfaces spitting salt water, swims back to the raft and climbs on. The sea tosses the raft about like autumn winds whirling thistle fluff along a road, as if all four winds were batting it back and forth.

barriers.quote: a sea broke over him
barriers.my_reading: a huge wave broke over him

barriers.quote: the raft reeled again
barriers.my_reading: The raft lurched violently; 'again' reads as 'a second time', though it has not reeled before.

barriers.quote: He let go the helm
barriers.my_reading: the steering gear (the 'rudder' of paragraphs 19-20), under a different name

barriers.quote: both sail and yard went over into the sea
barriers.my_reading: 'yard' is the sail's crossbar (the yardarm), not a garden or a measurement

barriers.quote: as autumn winds whirl thistledown round and round on a road
barriers.my_reading: The raft is tossed about like thistle fluff (seeds) blown round and round on a road.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Ino, daughter of Cadmus, also called Leucothea (once a mortal woman, now a sea goddess), sees Odysseus's plight and pities him. She rises from the waves like a seagull and sits on his raft.

Ino asks why Poseidon is so furious with him, but assures him that for all his raging Poseidon will not kill him. She tells him to strip, abandon the raft to the wind and swim for the Phaeacian coast, and gives him her magic veil to wrap round his chest for protection, telling him to throw it far back into the sea once he reaches land and then go away. She hands him the veil and dives back under the waves like a seagull.

barriers.quote: leave your raft to drive before the wind
barriers.my_reading: let the raft be blown along by the wind

barriers.quote: and then go away again
barriers.my_reading: Walk away from the shore once the veil is thrown back (perhaps without looking back); why 'again' is unclear.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus is suspicious that some god is luring him to his death by telling him to leave his raft, and the land still looks far off. He decides to stay on the raft as long as it holds together and only swim for it once the sea breaks it up.

barriers.quote: as long as her timbers hold together
barriers.my_reading: 'her' is the raft (boats called 'she'), not Ino, the 'she' of the previous sentence.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Before he can act, Poseidon sends a gigantic wave that smashes the raft apart like a pile of dry husks in a whirlwind; Odysseus straddles a single plank like a rider on a horse, strips off Calypso's clothes, ties Ino's veil under his arms and dives in to swim for shore. Poseidon watches and mutters mockingly that Odysseus can drift about until he meets some prosperous people, and cannot say he was let off lightly. Then Poseidon whips his horses and drives off to his palace at Aegae.

barriers.quote: a heap of dry chaff
barriers.my_reading: grain husks, very light and easily scattered

barriers.quote: till you fall in with well-to-do people
barriers.my_reading: Sarcastic: drift about until you meet some rich people (the Phaeacians) who will look after you; why their wealth is mentioned is not clear.

barriers.quote: he lashed his horses and drove to Aegae
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon has a horse-drawn chariot, apparently driven over the sea; it has not been mentioned before and is hard to picture.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena decides to help: she stops all the winds but one and stirs up a strong north wind to flatten the sea until Odysseus reaches the Phaeacians' land and safety.

barriers.quote: bound the paths of all the winds
barriers.my_reading: She shut the winds down, as if tying up the routes they travel along.

barriers.quote: a good stiff breeze from the North that should lay the waters
barriers.my_reading: A strong north wind meant to calm and flatten the waves ('lay' as in settle); it is unclear how a strong wind calms the sea.

paragraphs.paraphrase: He drifts for two days and nights in heavy swell, close to death; on the third morning the wind dies to a dead calm and, lifted on a swell, he sees land close by. He is as thankful as children whose father, long sick with an illness sent by some hostile spirit, finally starts to recover, and he swims hard for shore. But as he gets close he hears surf thundering against the rocks; everything is covered in spray and there is no harbour or shelter, only headlands, reefs and cliffs.

barriers.quote: as children rejoice when their dear father, who has long borne a sore affliction sent him by some angry spirit, begins to get better
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus's relief at seeing land is like children's joy when their long-sick father finally recovers.
barriers.note: long simile, hard to follow aloud; 'sore affliction' = painful illness

barriers.quote: where a ship might ride
barriers.my_reading: where a ship could lie safely at anchor

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus despairs that Zeus has let him see land but there is nowhere to get out: the rocks are sheer and smooth, with deep water and no foothold, and a wave may smash him against them as he climbs out. If he swims further along looking for a sloping beach or harbour, a storm may sweep him back out to sea, or a god may send a sea monster (Amphitrite breeds many), and he knows Poseidon hates him.

barriers.quote: some shelving beach
barriers.my_reading: a beach that slopes gently into the water

barriers.quote: for Amphitrite breeds many such
barriers.my_reading: Amphitrite seems to be a sea goddess who produces sea monsters; she is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: A wave hurls him at the rocks, and he would have been smashed if Athena had not prompted him to grab a rock with both hands and cling on, groaning, until the wave pulled back. But the backwash drags him out to sea again, stripping the skin off his hands on the rock (like an octopus pulled from its hole with pebbles still stuck to its suckers), and pulls him deep under water.

barriers.quote: tearing his hands as the suckers of an octopus are torn when someone plucks it from its bed, and the stones come up along with it
barriers.my_reading: When an octopus is pulled from its hiding place, stones stay stuck to its suckers; likewise bits of Odysseus's skin stay stuck to the rock. The two halves are reversed (stones come away with the octopus, skin stays behind on the rock), so it takes several reads.
barriers.note: hard to picture; 'its bed' = its hole or lair

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus would have died then, even against his fate, if Athena had not kept him thinking clearly: he swims back out beyond the breakers and along the coast, looking for a harbour or a point of land where the waves come in at an angle. Eventually he reaches a river mouth, free of rocks and sheltered from the wind, which seems the best place. Feeling the river's current, he prays silently.

barriers.quote: even in spite of his own destiny
barriers.my_reading: His fate was to get home, yet he could have died anyway, overriding fate; the idea that fate can be broken is puzzling.

barriers.quote: a spit that would take the waves aslant
barriers.my_reading: A narrow point of land where waves hit at an angle, so landing would be gentler.
barriers.note: 'spit' could be read as a roasting spit or saliva; 'aslant' is archaic

barriers.quote: He felt that there was a current, so he prayed inwardly
barriers.my_reading: The current tells him it is a river, and rivers have their own gods, so he prays to this one; the text does not say rivers are gods until paragraphs 33-34.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only that rivers were gods

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus prays to the unknown god of the river ('O King, whoever you may be') to save him from Poseidon's anger, arguing that any lost wanderer has a claim even on the gods. He comes to the river's stream as if clasping its knees, declares himself its suppliant and begs for mercy.

barriers.quote: Hear me, O King, whoever you may be
barriers.my_reading: He is addressing the god of the river, whose name he does not know; only 'your stream' later makes this clear.

barriers.quote: cling to the knees of your riverhood
barriers.my_reading: A formal begging gesture (clasping someone's knees) applied to a river; 'riverhood' is a made-up title like 'your majesty'.
barriers.note: sounds odd aloud; the knee-clasping custom is not explained

barriers.quote: I declare myself your suppliant
barriers.my_reading: someone who formally begs for protection and mercy
barriers.note: the custom and what it obliges are never explained; Book 6 depends on it

paragraphs.paraphrase: The river god holds back his current and calms the waves, bringing Odysseus safely into the river mouth, where his legs and hands give out; he is swollen, seawater streams from his mouth and nose, he cannot breathe or speak, and he faints from exhaustion. When he recovers he unties Ino's veil and throws it into the river's salty water, and a wave carries it back to Ino, who takes it in her hands. He leaves the river, lies down in the reeds and kisses the ground.

barriers.quote: the god stayed his stream
barriers.my_reading: the river god held back / stopped his current

barriers.quote: he took off the scarf that Ino had given him
barriers.my_reading: the same object called a 'veil' in paragraphs 25 and 27

barriers.quote: threw it back into the salt stream of the river
barriers.my_reading: Into the river mouth, where the water is salty; Ino had told him to throw it into the sea.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus weighs his options: if he stays by the river overnight, exhausted, the cold, the damp and the sharp dawn wind off the river may kill him. If he climbs into the woods and sleeps in a thicket, he will be warmer and rest, but a wild animal may eat him.

barriers.quote: If I stay here on the riverbed
barriers.my_reading: by the river, on the riverbank
barriers.note: 'riverbed' today means the bottom of the river channel

barriers.quote: the long watches of the night
barriers.my_reading: the long hours of the night ('watches' = divisions of the night)

paragraphs.paraphrase: He chooses the woods and, on high ground near the water, crawls under two olive bushes growing from one root (one wild, one cultivated), so thick that no wind, sun or rain gets through, where there is a deep layer of dead leaves. He lies down and heaps leaves over himself, the way someone living alone in the countryside buries a glowing ember in the ashes to keep a fire alive so he will not have to fetch fire from elsewhere. Athena then sends him sweet sleep, closing his eyes and easing his sorrows.

barriers.quote: the one an ungrafted sucker, while the other had been grafted
barriers.my_reading: One is a wild shoot from the root, the other a cultivated olive grafted onto it; together they make one dense bush.

barriers.quote: however squally
barriers.my_reading: however gusty or stormy

barriers.quote: hides a brand as fire-seed in the ashes to save himself from having to get a light elsewhere
barriers.my_reading: A 'brand' is a burning stick or ember; he buries it in ash to keep it smouldering so he can restart his fire. Odysseus buried in leaves is like that ember, keeping his spark of life alive.
barriers.note: 'brand' reads as a trademark; 'fire-seed' and 'get a light' need thought

book_level: Poseidon's grudge drives the whole second half (paragraphs 21-33) but no reason is ever given, and he is not called the sea god until paragraph 33; the 'suitors' (paragraph 2) are likewise never explained. Outside knowledge or earlier Books needed.

Hard to track which god is for or against Odysseus: Hermes says Athena wrecked the fleet (paragraph 8) though she is his champion in paragraphs 0-1, Calypso says Zeus's lightning did it (9), Odysseus blames Zeus for Poseidon's storm (22), then Athena rescues him (28-32).

The raft-building paragraph (19) is a wall of carpentry and sailing jargon (adze, augers, beam, ribs, gunwale, yardarm, wicker hurdles, braces and sheets); the 'raft' ends up sounding like a full ship and cannot be pictured. Sailing usage continues: 'a sea' for a wave, helm, yard, drive before the wind, ride, well-found.

Many unexplained names and titles: Tithonus, slayer of Argus, Orion (both a lover and a constellation), Iasion, Styx, Pleiads/Bootes/Wain/Oceanus, Amphitrite; two unglossed names for the Greeks in one speech (Danaans, Achaeans) plus the sons of Atreus, Priam and Achilles.

Several passages read as Victorian rather than modern English: 'not one of his subjects but has forgotten', 'would have it so', 'near of kin', 'laid their hands on the good things', 'presently' (= soon; 18, 31, 34), 'stayed his stream', 'lay the waters', 'watches of the night'.
Words whose modern meaning misleads: 'do their business' (5), 'victims' (8), 'prize money' (3), 'mischief' (13), 'sheets', 'hurdles' and 'yard' (19, 23), 'riverbed' (35), 'brand' (36).
The supplication custom (clasping someone's knees; 'suppliant', paragraph 33) appears without explanation, and Book 6 depends on it.
Long similes are hard to follow aloud, especially the octopus (31), whose two halves are reversed; also the sick father (29) and the buried ember (36).
